topics.title: AWS Organizations and multi-account strategy

kcs.statement: An AWS Organizations organization has one management account that creates it and pays its bills, plus member accounts. Each account stays a separate boundary for security and resources.
Organizational units (OUs) group accounts in a hierarchy under the organization root, and a policy attached to an OU applies to every account inside it.

A multi-account strategy puts environments, teams or workloads (for example production and development) in separate accounts. This limits the blast radius of mistakes and breaches and keeps access and costs separate.

AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM) shares resources such as subnets, transit gateways and License Manager configurations with other accounts or the whole organization, so they don't have to be duplicated.

serves.reason: Organizations and OUs come up in the governance questions of Domain 2 and the billing questions of Domain 4, and SCPs build on them

requires.reason: An organization is a collection of AWS accounts, so the learner must already know what an account is

problem_ideas: A startup has 40 engineers sharing one AWS account, and an intern deleted a production database while testing. Propose an account layout using OUs.

topics.title: Service control policies: guardrails for accounts

kcs.statement: A service control policy (SCP) sets the maximum permissions available in the accounts it is attached to. It grants nothing by itself, so a user still needs an IAM policy that allows the action.
An action in a member account is allowed only if both the SCPs and the IAM policies allow it. An explicit deny in either one blocks the action.
SCPs restrict every IAM user and role in a member account, including that account's root user. They never restrict the management account.

serves.reason: Exam questions about restricting what whole accounts may do have SCPs as the answer, and learners often confuse SCPs with IAM policies

requires.reason: SCPs are attached to the organization root, OUs or accounts, so the learner must know that hierarchy
Working out effective permissions combines an SCP with IAM policies and explicit deny

problem_ideas: An SCP allows only EC2 and S3. A user's IAM policy allows DynamoDB:*. Can the user create a DynamoDB table? Predict the result.

topics.title: Identity federation: sign in with an existing identity

kcs.statement: Identity federation lets users sign in through an external identity provider (a corporate directory, a SAML 2.0 or OIDC provider, or a social login) and receive temporary AWS credentials, so no long-term IAM user is created for each person.
Federation suits large or changing user populations: access is managed in one directory, nobody has long-term AWS keys to rotate, and disabling someone in the directory removes their AWS access.

serves.reason: Task Statement 2.3 explicitly asks learners to recognise types of identity management such as federation

requires.reason: Federated users get their AWS access by assuming roles with temporary credentials

topics.title: IAM Identity Center: one sign-in for many accounts

kcs.statement: IAM Identity Center (formerly AWS Single Sign-On) gives workforce users one sign-in portal for all the AWS accounts in an organization and for supported business applications.
IAM Identity Center grants access by assigning a user or group a permission set in a chosen account. The permission set becomes an IAM role in that account.
IAM Identity Center can use its own built-in directory, an external identity provider such as Okta or Microsoft Entra ID, or a Microsoft Active Directory as its source of identities.

topics.title: Cognito and Directory Service: app users and AD

kcs.statement: Amazon Cognito adds sign-up, sign-in and access control for the end users of your web and mobile apps (customer identity). It scales to millions of users and supports social and SAML logins.
Cognito user pools hold an application's customers, while IAM and IAM Identity Center hold the people who operate AWS. So 'users of our mobile app' points to Cognito, not to IAM users.

AWS Directory Service runs a managed Microsoft Active Directory in AWS (AWS Managed Microsoft AD) or connects to an existing on-premises AD (AD Connector), so workloads and users that depend on AD can work with AWS.

requires.reason: Cognito and Directory Service are both explained as identity sources for federation

problem_ideas: A fitness app expects 2 million users who sign in with Google or Apple. Name the service and explain why IAM users would be wrong.

topics.title: Encryption at rest and in transit

kcs.statement: Encryption at rest protects stored data, such as EBS volumes, S3 objects and RDS databases, so a copied disk, snapshot or backup can't be read without the key.
Encryption in transit protects data moving across a network, usually with TLS (HTTPS) for client traffic or IPsec for VPN tunnels.

Under the shared responsibility model, AWS provides the encryption features and some services encrypt by default (S3 has encrypted every new object since January 2023). The customer remains responsible for deciding how data is encrypted and who may use the keys.

serves.reason: Sorting security tasks between AWS and the customer and choosing KMS or ACM both depend on telling the two kinds of encryption apart
Task Statement 2.2 asks directly about encryption options at rest and in transit

topics.title: AWS KMS: managed encryption keys

kcs.statement: AWS KMS creates, stores and controls encryption keys and integrates with services such as S3, EBS and RDS, so those services can encrypt data with a KMS key without you ever handling the key material.
AWS managed keys are created and managed by AWS for a single service. Customer managed keys are created by you and give you control of the key policy, rotation and disabling or deleting the key.
KMS is a shared (multi-tenant) managed service: AWS runs the underlying hardware security modules, and access to each key is controlled by its key policy together with IAM policies.

serves.reason: KMS is one of the services the o3 product requires learners to match to a stated need

requires.reason: KMS keys exist to encrypt data at rest, so learners need that concept first

problem_ideas: A compliance team must be able to disable a key immediately and control who uses it. Choose between an AWS managed key and a customer managed key.

topics.title: CloudHSM: your own dedicated key hardware

kcs.statement: AWS CloudHSM provides dedicated, single-tenant hardware security modules in your VPC, validated at FIPS 140 Level 3, where only you manage the keys and HSM users (AWS cannot access the keys). Use it when a regulation requires customer-controlled HSMs.

requires.reason: CloudHSM is taught as the dedicated alternative to the shared KMS

topics.title: AWS Certificate Manager: free TLS certificates

kcs.statement: AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) provisions, manages and automatically renews public SSL/TLS certificates at no extra cost, for use with integrated services such as Elastic Load Balancing, CloudFront and API Gateway. This is how those services serve HTTPS (encryption in transit).

requires.reason: Certificates enable TLS, which is how data is encrypted in transit

topics.title: Secrets Manager: storing and rotating credentials

kcs.statement: AWS Secrets Manager stores credentials such as database passwords and API keys, encrypted with KMS. Applications retrieve them at runtime instead of having them hard-coded in source code or config files.

Secrets Manager can rotate secrets automatically on a schedule (with built-in support for RDS databases). Automatic rotation is the feature that sets it apart from Systems Manager Parameter Store in exam questions.

problem_ideas: A developer committed an RDS password to a public Git repository. Which service prevents this, and how?

topics.title: AWS Shield: DDoS protection, Standard vs Advanced

kcs.statement: A DDoS (distributed denial-of-service) attack floods a target with traffic from many sources to exhaust its capacity. Edge services such as CloudFront and Route 53, together with Auto Scaling, absorb much of it.
Shield Standard is turned on automatically for every AWS customer at no extra cost and protects against common network-layer and transport-layer (layer 3 and 4) DDoS attacks.

Shield Advanced is a paid subscription (about $3,000 a month per organization). It adds enhanced attack detection, 24/7 access to the Shield Response Team and cost protection for scaling charges caused by a DDoS attack.

serves.reason: Shield is one of the services the o3 product requires learners to match to a stated need

problem_ideas: A gaming company was hit by a 2 Tbps SYN flood and wants 24/7 expert help during attacks. Choose between Shield Standard and Shield Advanced.

topics.title: AWS WAF: filtering web requests at layer 7

kcs.statement: AWS WAF is a layer 7 web application firewall. Rules in a web ACL filter HTTP(S) requests, for example to block SQL injection or cross-site scripting, block specific IP addresses or countries, or rate-limit clients.
WAF protects web front doors such as CloudFront distributions, Application Load Balancers and API Gateway APIs. It cannot be attached to a Network Load Balancer or directly to an EC2 instance.

serves.reason: WAF is one of the services the o3 product requires learners to match to a stated need

topics.title: AWS CloudTrail: who did what, when

kcs.statement: AWS CloudTrail records API calls and account activity made through the console, CLI, SDKs or other AWS services: who made the call, what it was, when, and from which IP address. This record is used for auditing and investigations.
CloudTrail event history shows the last 90 days of management events at no charge. Keeping logs longer requires a trail that delivers log files to an S3 bucket.
CloudTrail answers 'who did what in the account' (API activity). VPC Flow Logs record network traffic, and CloudWatch records performance metrics and application logs.

serves.reason: CloudTrail is one of the services the o3 product requires learners to match to a stated need

topics.title: AWS Config: resource history and compliance rules

kcs.statement: AWS Config records the configuration of your resources over time, so you can see what a resource looked like at any point in time and what changed.

AWS Config rules check resources against desired settings (for example 'S3 buckets must not be public' or 'EBS volumes must be encrypted') and flag non-compliant resources. Remediation can be automated.
AWS Config answers 'what does this resource look like, and is it compliant?' CloudTrail answers 'who made the API call that changed it?'

serves.reason: Config is one of the services the o3 product requires learners to match to a stated need

requires.reason: The KC that separates Config from CloudTrail can only be checked once CloudTrail is known

topics.title: Amazon GuardDuty: intelligent threat detection

kcs.statement: Amazon GuardDuty is an intelligent threat detection service. It continuously analyzes CloudTrail events, VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs with machine learning and threat intelligence to find threats such as crypto-mining, compromised credentials or contact with known malicious IP addresses.
GuardDuty needs no agents and no log setup from you. Once enabled for an account (or a whole organization), it reads the log sources itself and produces security findings.

serves.reason: GuardDuty is one of the services the o3 product requires learners to match to a stated need

requires.reason: GuardDuty is defined by the logs it analyzes, and CloudTrail is the main one

topics.title: Inspector vs Macie: vulnerabilities vs sensitive data

kcs.statement: Amazon Inspector automatically scans EC2 instances, container images in ECR and Lambda functions for software vulnerabilities (CVEs) and unintended network exposure, and ranks its findings by risk.
Amazon Macie uses machine learning and pattern matching to discover and protect sensitive data, such as personally identifiable information (PII), stored in S3 buckets.
Inspector finds vulnerabilities in your workloads, Macie finds sensitive data in S3, and GuardDuty finds active threats in your logs.

serves.reason: Inspector and Macie are both in the list of services the o3 product requires learners to match

requires.reason: The three-way KC separating Inspector, Macie and GuardDuty needs GuardDuty first

topics.title: Security Hub and Detective: one view and root cause

kcs.statement: AWS Security Hub collects findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie and partner tools into a single view across accounts. It also runs automated checks against standards such as the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark and AWS Foundational Security Best Practices.
Amazon Detective analyzes and visualizes log data such as CloudTrail events, VPC Flow Logs and GuardDuty findings, so you can investigate the root cause and scope of a security issue.
GuardDuty detects threats, Security Hub gives one prioritized view of security posture across accounts, and Detective investigates a specific finding in depth.

topics.title: Compliance programs and regional requirements

kcs.statement: AWS takes part in compliance programs and certifications such as ISO 27001, SOC 1/2/3, PCI DSS, FedRAMP and HIPAA eligibility. These cover AWS's infrastructure, not the customer's workload, which the customer must still make compliant.
Compliance needs depend on geography and industry (GDPR for EU personal data, HIPAA for US health data, PCI DSS for card payments), and data-residency rules decide which Regions a workload may use.
Not every AWS service is in scope for every compliance program. Before using a service for a regulated workload, check AWS's 'Services in Scope by Compliance Program' list.

Suspected abuse coming from AWS resources (spam, port scanning, DDoS, malware hosting) is reported to the AWS Trust & Safety team through the abuse report form or abuse@amazonaws.com.

topics.title: Choosing a security service for a requirement

kcs.statement: For access needs: workforce users across many accounts → IAM Identity Center; end users of an app → Cognito; existing Microsoft AD → Directory Service; limit what whole accounts can do → service control policies.
For data protection: manage encryption keys → KMS; dedicated single-tenant HSM → CloudHSM; SSL/TLS certificates → ACM; store and rotate credentials → Secrets Manager; find PII in S3 → Macie.

For threats: DDoS → Shield; SQL injection, XSS or IP and geo blocking → WAF; firewall rules across accounts → Firewall Manager; threats in logs → GuardDuty; software vulnerabilities → Inspector; one view of findings → Security Hub; root-cause investigation → Detective.
For audit and compliance: who made an API call → CloudTrail; resource configuration history and compliance rules → AWS Config; AWS's own compliance reports and the BAA → AWS Artifact.

serves.reason: This topic is the o3 product itself: naming the security service that meets a stated need and ruling out the nearest distractor
Security service selection questions make up a large share of Domain 2 (30% of the exam)

requires.reason: Telling threat services apart needs the full detection set: GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, Security Hub and Detective
Telling audit services apart needs Config and CloudTrail

For each scenario, name the right service and explain why the nearest distractor is wrong (WAF vs Shield, Config vs CloudTrail, KMS vs CloudHSM).
A breach timeline: suspicious login → data exfiltration → audit. Assign a service to each phase.
A fintech's checklist: encrypt data, rotate DB passwords, block SQL injection, prove PCI to auditors. Map each item.
Find the one wrong answer in a list of 8 requirement → service pairs.
A mock exam item has four plausible security services. Eliminate three using keywords.
